utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, we're late starting. There seems to be a breakdown in communication with the video booth, but we're now ready. So if you could make your re-examination even quicker, please, so we can get on to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would ask the registrar, please, to distribute to the bench and to counsel and the witness a quick summary that will make this very quick. Also, while that's being distributed, if I just may bring to the attention of the court and the court reporters, Ms. Verhaag indicated that on page 9671 of yesterday's transcript, there is an error in the date. The line should read: "... recollection of conversations that occurred in February '94," but it says "February '93," which is not the time frame during which Lieutenant-Colonel Carter was in Bosnia. If it's possible just to make that correction, we would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Carter, a number of questions concerning the role of Dario Kordic in the various governmental structures of Herceg-Bosna were posed to you yesterday, and in review, there were many inaccuracies in the questioning. In order to clear this up, I would ask that everybody take a look at the binder in front of him and pay only attention to those pages that have yellow tabs. I preface this by saying that because of the short time frame, an official translation in the Serbo-Croat of the Narodni List has not been obtained; it has been requested both in French and English. What we have been able to do, if the Court will grant us this, is just to have not a totally accurate, but reasonable summary, and we will put in as quickly as possible the official one. It's just the time frame that's made it impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Carter, if you can look at the first tab, please. The Narodni List, of course, is one of the documents with which International Community people are familiar, as it is the Official Gazette of Herceg-Bosna, both the Community and the Republic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLOYD CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the first tabbed English page, it says page 18, number 1, "October 1993, Official Gazette of the Community of Herceg-Bosna." Can you indicate, please, under "Decision", what that decision concerns and what Dario Kordic has to do with that decision?

utterances.speaker: FLOYD CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reading there, it indicates that he has been nominated chamber of deputies, CRHB, that is, for the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, from Busovaca, as president; and Bozo Rajic from Kupres as member.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you turn to the next page, which has some highlighting on it as well, it says "Article 2" and it talks about when it goes into effect, and that indicates it should go in on the date of adoption; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLOYD CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The next decision on that same page, although it does not have a tab -- the tab is on the next page in English -- indicates that it is a decision on the election of members for the Committee for Internal and Foreign Policy and National Security of the HR-HB, Chamber of Deputies, which is another name for the House of Representatives. Do you see Dario Kordic's name on the next page?

utterances.speaker: FLOYD CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Looking at the next tab in English -- may I point out to the Chamber and to counsel that the English is always first and the Serbo-Croat is later. There are other documents which are not tabbed but are relevant, but for the purposes of this examination, I think it's sufficient to go to the highlighted ones. On the next English tab, dated March 1994 -- it is page 342, number 8 of the Narodni List, or the Official Gazette -- what does the decision indicate about Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: FLOYD CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision on election, vice-president chamber of deputies, CRHB, as vice-president, Dario Kordic, from Busovaca, and Vlado Santic from Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next English language tab shows June 1995, the Official Gazette of HR-HB, page 403, number 17. What does the decision concern? It's in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must object to this. This is, A, beyond the scope of our cross-examination and, B, concerns matters that occurred, apparently, in 1995, which is years after the end of the period covered by the amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's all part of the picture. Whether it is of any weight or significance will be a matter for us to decide in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Carter, would you continue, please.

utterances.speaker: FLOYD CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Announcement of the members of the Presidential Council of HR-HB to include Dario Kordic and Tihomir Blaskic as members.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The next English page, please, it says page 434, number 18 of the Official Gazette, June 1995. What does the decision concern?

utterances.speaker: FLOYD CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Relief of duty of members of commissional elections, chamber of deputies. Relieved of duty, Dario Kordic as president --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: FLOYD CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following persons relieved of duty: Dario Kordic as president, Hudic as vice-president, and Rajic as member.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And Dario Kordic and Bozo Rajic were the vice-presidents during the HZ-HB period; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: FLOYD CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The next page, please, in English would be page 436, number 18 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please slow down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The interpreters are having difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. I'll slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The next decision, page 436, number 18, June 1995. Could you tell us what it concerns, please?

utterances.speaker: FLOYD CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Appointment of members for internal and foreign policy and national security of the HRHB Chamber of Deputies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And is Kordic named there?

utterances.speaker: FLOYD CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He is named as President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The next page, please, page 538, number 23 of the Official Gazette of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosnia, July 1995. The decision concerns?

utterances.speaker: FLOYD CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It concerns Dario Kordic's relief of duty as vice-president of the Herceg Republic Chamber of Deputies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, you indicated yesterday that you viewed the type of authority of Mr. Kordic as evolutionary. And in furtherance of that evolution, if you will turn to the next tabbed English page, which is labelled November 1992, Official Gazette of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. That would be HZHB, number 7, page 17. Would you please read the decision?

utterances.speaker: FLOYD CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That decision appoints members of the HVO and includes Dario Kordic as a member of the personnel commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of the HVO HZHB personnel commission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLOYD CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And then finally -- actually, that is it. Therefore, yesterday the assertion that was made that Dario Kordic only held one position in the government structure of HRHB prior to February of '94 was inaccurate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLOYD CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That's argumentative and a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I agree. It's for us to make a decision about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry. If I may just rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There were positions that were held?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Ms. Somers, please. Could you slow down, Ms. Somers. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Carter, I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: FLOYD CARTER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he held various positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. My apologies. Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Colonel, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the next witness to be brought in, let me deal with two matters. First of all, a memorandum which has been sent to me on behalf of the interpreters. They request that, whenever possible, counsel, when handing out documents, make sure that three additional copies go to the interpretation booths. This was apparently mentioned to you when you were speaking to them at the beginning. And if that is not possible, that at least there is a copy put on the electronic monitor. Bear in mind the difficulty which the interpreters have in a case of this sort and also their crucial role in the case. And so would counsel kindly do all they can to make their job as easy as possible. The other matter concerns the week of the 29th of November, when there will be sittings in the afternoon in the case of Simic, which means that this case will not be able to sit. What has been agreed is that on Monday, the 29th of November, and Tuesday, the 30th of November, and possibly, and I am told probably by some, on Wednesday, the 1st of December, this case won't sit. So those two first days that I mentioned, definitely, and a possibility of a third day. We'll sit this afternoon till a quarter past five and take a break at a suitable moment. If we could have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Are you, in fact, Alastair Duncan, now a General in the British army, born in 1952 in Norfolk, England; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Duncan, before you begin to testify, could you tell me, please, whether you were able to read the summary of your statements that was made, starting with your statement in April of 1997 and your testimony in the Blaskic case on the 3rd of June 1998? Were you able to read that document?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you agree with what's stated in the summary?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Duncan, did you join the British army in 1970?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And since that time you were a Commander of military operations at various levels, in fact all levels, from the platoon to the company, battalion and brigade, and even division; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Is it also true that you were responsible for tactics and command duties of commanders in the British army?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Were you trained at the Shrivenham College, training college, as well as the Camberley College?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was taught at both establishments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During your career, did you become a specialist and command the responsibilities and duties of unit commanders and, more specifically, in infantry units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Duncan, from May 1993 to November 1993, as a Lieutenant-Colonel, were you the commanding officer of the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment of Yorkshire, at that time stationed in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And you replaced Colonel Bob Stewart, who was responsible for the Cheshire brigade, and who left Central Bosnia at the same time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: It was on the 11th of May, 1993 that you took over your command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: The 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the days preceding that date, that is, from the 5th to the 11th of May, did you already have the possibility of becoming familiar with the zone that you were going to command by making various on-site visits to unit commanders who were available?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During the visit, did you have the chance to go to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went to Ahmici briefly with Colonel Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You had already come to Central Bosnia in January and February of 1993 on a reconnaissance mission in order to prepare your future mission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Your area of responsibility for your regiment covered the Prozor region, Gornji Vakuf, Zenica, Vitez, and the way up to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Was your regiment composed of several companies, two mixed companies in Vitez, one in Gornji Vakuf and one in Tuzla, with your headquarters being in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During the period when you held that command, General Duncan, did you note various phases on the ground, particularly that in May and June 1993 the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had made substantial gains in territory in the Vitez and Busovaca areas?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did you also note that in July 1993 that the conflict extended into the Gornji Vakuf zone, where there was very heavy fighting, and from that period onwards the situation became static around Vitez, Busovaca and Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I would like us to focus now on the Vitez area, the Vitez pocket. That Vitez area was of materiel, political and strategic interest; is that correct? That is, for the Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you tell us why specifically that zone was important for the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I believe this zone represented an area of Croat -- Bosnian Croat territory, which was claimed by the Bosnian Croats as for theirs, and they wished to keep that territory. The area was of military significance in that it dominated the Lasva Valley in that part of Central Bosnia and created a pocket, along with the other pockets, which was preventing the Bosnian Muslim army from making further advances to the south and taking more territory. The area had a spinal road through it and the defence was conducted with some territorial forces which held the ground throughout the pockets and then using the spinal road to reinforce the area, in a similar fashion to the way that troops were able to move very quickly by train in the First World War to plug the holes before breakthroughs. And that defence was conducted with extreme success by the Bosnian Croat army in that pocket, the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In Vitez was there also any types of industries that were of particular interest to both the parties?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: There was an ammunition, an armament factory in Vitez, which I believe held large quantities of explosives, which was of strategic significance both to the Croat and Muslim forces. Furthermore, in Novi Travnik area there was an arms factory which was also of strategic significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The units of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army were interested in those factories, and of course the HVO was opposed to their capturing those industries; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As regards the HVO forces that we are speaking about, what is your opinion as to the quality of the equipment that the HVO had as regards communications?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: The HVO had quite sophisticated communications, consisting of telephone and fax facilities, as well as, I believe, satellite phone facilities, and also some what one might term walkie-talkies, for tactical command on the ground, although I believe these were linked by repeaters and thus they were able to communicate throughout their operational zone with this equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did the HVO also have equipment in case there were electricity cuts?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I believe they had generators to sustain their communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As regards the operations of that HVO army, you concluded that that army operated like any other army in the world, even if it had an operating system which is somewhat particular to it, because it was based on a territorial organisation?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The HVO army in the Vitez pocket was organised very much on territorial lines, in that some troops were allocated various sectors to which they would be permanently attached. There were then manoeuvre elements behind that could reinforce. And although the soldiers lived at home with their weapons and equipment, they were very quick to mobilise and plug gaps and followed a very good chain of command. This is similar to modern armies in Norway, Sweden and Switzerland, who have a territorial-based army which is every bit as efficient, in fact in many cases more efficient, because troops are already in their battle positions rather than have troops deployed in barracks, where they have to be moved out to engage enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As regards the military equipment that that HVO army had, were you able to see that the army also had effective operational equipment, modern equipment?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they had modern equipment, which had formerly belonged to the Yugoslav army and was now theirs, of up to 152-millimetre-calibre field guns, mortars of up to 120 millimetre, machine-guns and anti-aircraft guns. And it would appear they had sufficient ammunition for that weapon system as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Still speaking about the HVO army's organisation, did you know that there was a disciplinary regulation or code which had been set up or drafted for the organisation of those units?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. I understood that there was a military code for the HVO, and I have seen throughout the time an English translation of that code. The code covers all the normal functions and requirements of a military code to enable an army to operate both administratively and on the field in operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I would like to show you a document, General. This was a document published in the Narodni List in September 1992 and it's dated 3 July 1992 and signed by the President Mate Boban. This is Exhibit Z200-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to say for the transcript that the document is 3 July, 3 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: General, would you have a look at that document, the English version of the document, and tell us whether that corresponds to the Code of Military Discipline that you have just spoken to us about.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is the Code of Military Discipline for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony before the Office of the Prosecutor in April of 1997, you put forth a document, which was called the battle order, in military language, which was prepared by the intelligence officer of your regiment, Mr. Simon Harrison. I would like to show you the document and would then ask you to make some comments about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is referenced Exhibit Z2653, 2653.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The document is almost at the end of the pile of documents that was given to you.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we put that on the ELMO, please. Could we put the document on the ELMO, please. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Is this document the one that you gave to our investigators in April of 1997, General?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is, and I've signed the top right-hand corner to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The document was drafted by the intelligence officer of your regiment, Mr. Harrison, at that time. Could you tell us what information this document was based on?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This document was based on information that was, firstly, handed over to us from the previous battalion, that is, Colonel Bob Stewart and the Cheshire Regiment; secondly, from visits by my officers around the area to brigades, formations, and troops, and also visits to headquarters by myself and my liaison officers. Thus we were able to compile this document and maintain it as accurately as we could, keeping it up to date throughout our time in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: On the first page of the document, we see the operational group commands of the HVO, as well as the various brigades, which were distributed through your area of responsibility and even beyond; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As regards the second, third, and fourth pages, they deal with the Bosnia-Herzegovina army units and the 3rd Corps, in particular, which was in Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately when that document was prepared, stating that in the lower right corner, we see the date of 14 June 1993 as being the date when the Kakanj Brigade surrendered to the Bosnian army forces.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This document would have been prepared and finalised shortly after that time, after we had received that information, and then my officer, Captain Simon Harrison, would have done an update; therefore, the date of the 14th of June is quite significant and places it around and about that time, perhaps slightly later than the 14th, to allow for the events to filter through to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In respect of the two accused, their names appear on the document; that is, the accused Mario Cerkez, which is somewhat cut off because the copy isn't very good, and we apologise for that, in the left part, for the Vitez Brigade --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: -- and we see the name of the accused Dario Kordic on the document as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where, Mr. Lopez-Terres, are we finding this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the accused Mario Cerkez, that is to be found in the lower left part. There is the mention of Viteska. The "Vit" is hard to read. And you've got the name of Cerkez, which you see there, and then furthest to the left, under the Operational Group 1, and right next to the Frankopan Brigade where there was a cross put. As regards the accused Dario Kordic, that also was in the left part of this document, in the first rectangle of that left part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: General Duncan, as we said, this is a battle order which is to be used purely by the military; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct. It's a battle order going down as far as the brigade level, and I carried a copy of this in my pocket during my time in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As regards a military document, could you explain to us why, on this upper-left part that we've just spoken about, we see a rectangle in which is the name of Mr. Kostroman, Valenta, Dario Kordic, and the name of the Bosnian Croat party, the HDZ? These are political structures; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I should explain that the box in the centre, the "OPs Zone of Central Bosnia," the top centre, this document describes the hierarchy of military units down to brigade size, and therefore you have three basic levels. The op zone at the top, which was the higher command; below that, the three operational groups, 1, 2, and 3; and below that, a number of named brigades formed up. This gives the skeleton of the key units which formed the op zone of Central Bosnia, commanded at that stage by Tihomir Blaskic, and you will see his name under the central box. On the left and right of that central box are dotted lines which connect the two dotted boxes, the one on the left entitled "HDZ" and the one on the right, the "BiH HVO Joint Command." These two boxes are included because of the political nature of the HVO command in that area, in that there was a clear link, in our minds, between the political and the military, and that's why those lines are dotted. Therefore, the influence from both the HDZ and the joint command would come into that central zone in the middle. That box on the left-hand side is not for specific command over those units there, more for influence into the centre. I could, perhaps, explain the relationship between that box on the left with "HDZ," and underneath it "Dario Kordic," and the "OPs Zone" box in the middle with Tihomir Blaskic. The box in the middle is for the operations; that is Blaskic's task. The box on the left was for the planning of those operations; that was Dario Kordic's task. The box in the middle is for the external fighting of the battle with all those forces underneath it. The box on the left is for internal business within the Vitez pockets and the other pockets that existed at that time. The box in the middle is for action, if you like, and the box on the left is for doctrine. The box in the middle is for the purely military aspects of business and the one on the left for the politics. So I hope that explains more clearly the relationship between those boxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: On the similar document relating to the 3rd Corps, we see the descriptions only of the military units. There is no equivalence in the Bosnian army of that kind of political presence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Sir, that is correct. We do not have a box to the right or left of that for the reason that the BiH, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the mainly Muslim army, did not have those same political connections, and I believe that is partly due to the fact that there was a clear link between the activities of the HVO and Croatia itself and the HV; whereas the Bosnian Muslim army, the BiH, did not obviously have links with anyone external to Bosnia of a political nature, in the same fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: On the same descriptive document, we do not see units like the military police units or the special units, such as the Vitezovi. Does that mean for you that those units were outside that command structure?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: No, sir. This document is specifically to cover the main military units and not supporting units; therefore, you can say it's a rather coarse, not a finely detailed, document. But this is how we would show, in the British army, an orbit of friendly or enemy forces, or even neutral forces. We would, therefore, not show supporting engineers, supporting artillery units, supporting manoeuvre units, or any other special units, such as military police or other supporting units. They would simply be accepted and attached and moved as required. We might have shown them on a separate sheet as what we would call corps troops available for deployment throughout the area, but I didn't in this case, and we didn't have the detail on the sheets, just, as I called it, course groupings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The influence of politics over the military matters, you yourself, such as your liaison officers in the field, were you able to see that at all levels, including the level of municipalities and brigades? I would like to show you a document in that respect. This is document Z969. It is a report, a milinfosum of 24 May 1993. That is document 969. Would you please read the second paragraph of the document, General Duncan?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir: "The ECMM LO confirms the growing problems of Vitez by reporting that the meeting of the local commission was the most unproductive yet. At the meeting, Mario Cerkez stated that Mario Skopljak, the mayor, had recommended that he stop attending the joint commission as it was clearly not working. Comment: That the HDZ controls the actions of the HVO is becoming increasingly apparent. Comment ends."

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. In the report that came from your regiment, do you find the confirmation of the idea that there was an influence of the political side on the military side, including on the brigade level, such as here in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir, and this was just one example of that particular influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go back to a point that we've already referred to, that is, the military police units in particular. These military police units do not appear on the battle order that we've just spoken about. According to the information that you were able to get at that time, could you tell us what authority or authorities these units were subordinate to?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: The military police, within the op zone, would be subordinate to the commanders within that op zone, either working directly for the commanders at the highest level -- that is, both externally for Tihomir Blaskic, or internally, I believe, for Dario Kordic -- and then down through this hierarchy, they would be assigned as required to meet tasks. When such a unit is assigned, it comes under the operational task of that particular organisation, so that there is one commander for that organisation. It clearly would not be acceptable, in a wartime situation, to have a unit come into one's area of responsibility which had to be fed, clothed, supplied with ammunition, and looked after, if you were not also responsible for its actions; otherwise, you could find it acting as against your plans as opposed to with your plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You have just said that the military police units could be subordinate both or successively to Dario Kordic, Tihomir Blaskic, or possibly, if I understood you correctly, Mario Cerkez, who was the brigade commander, if those units were acting within his zone of responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes. Exactly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I would like to show you another report that your regiment drafted, that is, Exhibit Z881,1, and I would say that this report is dated 3 May 1993. It is a mistake. It shouldn't say "3 May". That was a typographical error made by the regiment at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to this document, we've not seen it before; that's not a real problem, but we object to the document coming into evidence for the truth of the matters asserted on page 2. The subjunctive phraseology of those questions obviously consists of speculation, and we don't know whose speculation is reflected on page 2. In the absence of a foundation, we would object to this document being admitted for the truth of those propositions which are contested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can give evidence about the document. What weight it has will depend upon our understanding of the evidence and our decision as to its value. Yes, it is admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: General, could you take a look at the second page of the document, the document which was just mentioned by Mr. Sayers, that is, the paragraph dealing with Vitez. Does this document, in fact, come from your regiment, that is, report number 35 of your regiment?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does. It was prepared on an almost daily basis by Captain Simon Harrison, assisted by warrant officer McLeod, who were responsible for this. The Vitez LO mentioned in paragraph 4 was a Captain Whitworth, and he had confirmed by visiting those details listed under there. And where it says "Comment," that is the comment by a Captain Simon Harrison to do with that information. He has made a comment on the information, and that is clearly separate from the statement. This document represented every day to me, which recorded the day's events, and it would then be distributed around all units on all parts of my command in order that everybody should be kept up to date with events and changes of details as they occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In that Kordic's authority over the military police and the estimate that you made, does it correspond to the information that you and the regiment had available at that time in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, it does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, the document says they apparently come under the direct control of Dario Kordic. What information would you have had that would substantiate that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It would be substantiated by visits of my officers to those units. One of their tasks was to work out and complete the sheets of who worked for who in the area. And they wouldn't gather that over one visit; it would be gathered over a number of visits, talking to both local people, officers in the units involved, and as many other sources as we could put together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could you give us a practical example of an event that would indicate the control or some fact that would indicate the control?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Much of -- it would be difficult to give a concrete fact that would originate control. And I would have to cast my mind back over events that took place to find one. And regrettably, nothing springs to mind immediately. But the officers and the LO's would obviously not put that information in if they didn't think it was of value. And at this stage in June that year, it was of value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: General, perhaps you anticipated the question that I was going to ask you. The incident of June '93, that is the Convoy of Joy, couldn't that be, for instance, an illustration, example of what we are talking about? We shall come back to that incident, so if you would only briefly touch upon it now.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: During the incident involved on which we called the Convoy of Joy, there was an occasion where the road was blocked by both civilians, local HVO soldiers and local police. I quoted the name of Commander Blaskic in saying I had his authority to come through. This was refused and I was only allowed to go through, they said, if I had the express authority of Dario Kordic. Thus, those units therefore were under the express command of Dario Kordic and would not take orders from Tihomir Blaskic. So I hope that briefly gives an example, which I'm afraid I couldn't call to mind before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: We shall come back to that incident and discuss about 10th of June, 1993, and we shall talk about it in greater detail during your testimony. However, during your period of command there, you met various personalities in Central Bosnia -- the accused Dario Kordic, Anto Valenta, Colonel Blaskic -- and I believe that you are also familiar with the name of Mario Cerkez, but you do not remember meeting him as a brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's quite correct. Whilst I am familiar with the name Mario Cerkez, I do not remember or recall ever meeting him when I was in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: But there were, of course, according to the organisational chart, there were responsibilities, and they -- your subordinates were directly in contact and communicated with the brigade commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. What I wanted to do in my relations with people is not to duplicate activity, because my area of responsibility, as you've heard, stretched a huge distance. And therefore it was important that we didn't duplicate our effort. I elected that it would be correct for me to speak at the level of the Ops Zone Commander, that is, to Tihomir Blaskic and Dario Kordic, and below that my company commanders would take the next level down. Below that, my liaison officers would take a level below that. So that we had a structure to go and find information and come back and monitor what was going on. Because what I didn't want to do was have a stream of people visiting various organisations during the day, which, frankly, would have been upsetting for them and a nuisance. And that also that system I adopted enabled a good flow of information between my officers and the single units in some cases that they were assigned to, or a town, and it may be in some cases I said: Your responsibility is Vitez, your responsibility is Busovaca or your responsibility is Novi Travnik. It was an attempt to separate out and make sure we had some efficient links established.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Those liaison officers in the regiment, one of them was Mark Bower; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Bower was one of my key liaison officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And on the 9th of May, 1993, if I am correct, you met for the first time the accused Dario Kordic, accompanied by Tihomir Blaskic, and you met in the Vitez Hotel, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you tell us very briefly on whose initiative was the meeting called?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: The meeting was called on the initiative of Colonel Bob Stewart, because on the 9th of May I had not yet taken over command of the troops, the British troops in the Vitez area. The purpose of the meeting was to introduce me to Tihomir Blaskic and see his headquarters, and it was also an opportunity for Colonel Stewart to question Blaskic about the events of Ahmici, which had taken place a couple of weeks or so before. That was the purpose of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As far as you could understand, Colonel Stewart and Tihomir Blaskic had already met before and discussed the massacre at Ahmici, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, they had indeed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: A correction. Excuse me. It seems that on the transcript the name of the liaison officer who was mentioned, by whom I mentioned, is Lee Whitworth, and it seems that it is missing. So I would just like -- Lee Whitworth and Angus Hay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You mentioned Mark Bower.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mark Bower. [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we've got evidence about these things anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Lopez-Terres. It seems that the witness answered only with regard to Mr. Bower, saying that he was one of his most important liaison officers, but he did not comment on other names. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Lee Whitworth and Angus Hay were also officers, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could clarify, because these officers were obviously under my command. Mark Bower was a captain whose primary responsibility was for the Red Cross and also to see whether aid was distributed around the area. Captain Hay, Angus Hay, his primary responsibility was for the Vitez area itself. Later on he was to hand over to Captain Whitworth. And those three captains were part of my team of liaison officers at that time. I trust that makes that clear, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And during this meeting on the 9th of May 1993, was Dario Kordic in a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I don't believe that Dario Kordic was at the beginning of the meeting, but during the meeting he came in. He was dressed in a camouflage pattern material, without a hat, and with no badges of rank. When he came in, the proceedings were stopped and he was briefly introduced as Dario Kordic. I was given to understand that he was, how shall I say, of Colonel status and therefore he had a status, although not an official rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the course of this meeting, the item of the village of Ahmici was referred to. Could you please tell us briefly what explanations were made by Colonel Blaskic as regards the perpetrators of the massacre at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Colonel Stewart accused Colonel Blaskic of being directly responsible for the Ahmici massacre. This he denied and he gave the reasons -- or the responsibility for the attack on Ahmici to three sources: The first was Serb extremists, who would have had to have come an awful long way to get there; the second was Muslims attacking their own Muslims; and the third was Muslims dressed up in HVO uniform. Both Colonel Stewart and myself found these explanations as to who had done the attacking and those responsibilities completely unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the course of this meeting Colonel Blaskic admitted that the village of Ahmici was within his responsibility, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As far as you know, General, was the village of Ahmici also in the area of responsibility of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was very close to Vitez, six to eight hundred yards, from memory of that map of that area. It was certainly not far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During those explanations made by Colonel Blaskic, do you remember if the accused Dario Kordic intervened, perhaps intervened perhaps to add something to these explanations or comment on them?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I don't recollect that he made any comment at that stage. I think one would describe him as being very much in the back seat of that meeting, which was really a meeting between myself, Colonel Stewart and Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Would you know if Colonel Stewart had invited Dario Kordic to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: No, sir, I wasn't aware of that. We were merely -- the plan had been to visit Commander Blaskic in his headquarters, and he was not directly invited, certainly not by Colonel Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And in the course of that meeting, you and Colonel Stewart, did you indicate to Colonel Blaskic that the Muslims in Ahmici were seen escorted by HVO soldiers and then taken to Vitez, where they were detained, and what did Colonel Blaskic answer after he received that information from you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: He answered that -- well, first of all, he was somewhat reluctant to answer and denied that there were HVO escorting those prisoners, but Colonel Stewart was quite emphatic, because he had personally seen these people been escorted. And one of the reasons put forward by Colonel Blaskic was that this was for the safety of those Muslims. This surprised both Colonel Stewart and myself, because we weren't particularly sure why Muslims should be kept safe from other Muslims. And surely it would be better if the HVO forces were involved in guaranteeing protection for the Croats in the area of Ahmici, rather than the Muslims, since it was the Muslims who had been attacked, and not the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did Colonel Blaskic mention during that meeting at some time the presence of some extremists in this sector of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: He did mention extremists, yes. At this meeting, and many after, meetings afterwards, the word "extremists" was used a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did you know at that time who was Colonel Blaskic referring to at that moment?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I should state that Colonel Blaskic was clearly referring in his mind to those people who had done the massacre at Ahmici and labelling them as extremists. I came to realise over the succeeding months that this excuse was always used by commanders to deny that they had anything to do with operations. But I found it very strange in such a small place as the Vitez pocket, where there was a military, a firm and an efficient military control, both externally in the defence of the pocket and internally from the HVO military police, civilian police and others, that such a situation of extremists could occur. My conclusion, therefore, was that there weren't extremists at all. There were Croat forces who were being directed from central command to carry out various actions, as and when required by either the military or the political.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, if you are going to move on to another topic, this might be a convenient moment to take a break for a quarter of an hour. One matter to consider is this: that I understand this witness can only be here for today and tomorrow. The position tomorrow is that we shall only be sitting in the afternoon. The hearing will be restricted by the fact that the case I am sitting on in the morning is liable to go on till 2.00. So at the earliest, we will not be able to begin until 2.45. That being so, at the present rate of going, it seems very unlikely that we are going to get through this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have already envisaged that possibility, which I know Duncan, Mr. President, General Duncan has confirmed to me that he would not be available after tomorrow afternoon, and, if need be, we have already envisaged another date when he could again appear before the Chamber to finish his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Five past 4.00, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before we continue with the examination, the testimony, I spoke with Mr. Sayers about the length of cross-examination, and the Defence counsel have told me that they are envisaging a whole day for the cross-examination of this witness. The witness, before he made his solemn declaration, told me that he would be ready to come back on the 25th of November or the 1st of December, and on the basis of what you have told us now, the 1st of December -- evidently, on the 1st of December, we would not be sitting, but we shall have to discuss with this witness a day when he will be able to come again. So if you would allow me, I should like to consult the witness on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you can do that, you've certainly got leave to do that, but how long do you anticipate being in chief? Can you finish that by tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lopez-Terres, how much longer is the direct examination going to last?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe we shall need perhaps about a quarter of an hour tomorrow to complete the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that means that the cross-examination can't start tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you say one day, if you have the whole afternoon tomorrow for the cross-examination, then you will not need another afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that is a question that you should ask the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I am asking both. Does that mean that tomorrow afternoon, Mr. Sayers, you will use for cross-examination? Because the examination-in-chief will take only ten minutes, a quarter of an hour tomorrow, so you will begin to cross-examine the General tomorrow, and therefore you will need only another afternoon to complete your cross-examination. I believe that would be more useful to us. So would you agree with me, Mr. Sayers, that you will need, after tomorrow, only another afternoon to complete your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would like to agree. I can't be absolutely certain, without hearing precisely what the General has to say, Your Honour. But clearly we respect the General's tight schedule, clearly we have to work around the General's schedule, but by the same token, I would stress -- and I'm sure this point is not lost on the Trial Chamber -- that the evidence of this witness is very significant. He's an extremely important witness; in fact, as far as I can tell, the first witness who has come forward with concrete evidence on the matters charged in the amended indictment, rather than speculation. So it's important for us not to rush through the cross-examination of this witness, as perhaps we have done with other more peripheral witnesses. I want to be certain that we go through the General's testimony very carefully. Many of the issues upon which he has testified consist of matters of opinion, maybe legitimate, and we have to examine the basis for those opinions, and there are a number of documents that we have to examine with this witness. But I would certainly think that the cross-examination would not last more than one entire trial day, and I have consulted with my colleagues representing Mr. Cerkez and they have told me that they anticipate that the questions they have for the General would last perhaps a half an hour, perhaps 45 minutes, depending on how long I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Certainly we will finish the examination-in-chief, Mr. Lopez-Terres, and you can put your mind to that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: General Duncan, before we took our break, we were speaking about the meeting between Colonel Blaskic and Dario Kordic. During that meeting, Colonel Blaskic committed himself to making an investigative report about the events in Ahmici and that everything would be done before the 25th of May, 1993. As far as you know, was an investigative report ever prepared, or did you ever learn about such a report during the seven months that you were there?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Sir, it's my understanding at that meeting that the date, the 25th of May, was produced for -- was suggested to be the date when that report should be produced, with the evidence fresh in people's minds. At that time, and since then, I have not seen any report produced by the Bosnian Croat forces, the HVO, of events in Ahmici at all. There's been no report, to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Four days after that meeting, that is, on the 13th of May, 1993, you had quite a long meeting with Anto Valenta in his office at Colonel Blaskic's headquarters in the Hotel Vitez. We're going to speak about that meeting. Mr. Valenta gave you a book on that day and also explained some of his ideas to you about how certain movements of populations would be possible in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Could we speak about that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I went to visit Mr. Valenta in his office in the Hotel Vitez, in the centre of Vitez town. He then wished to present to me the contents, a brief resume, of the book he wrote in 1991. This book concerned the movement of -- or the problems, as he saw it, rather, in Bosnia as a whole, and he presented to me what he saw as a number of solutions to this problem. I have to say I found his solutions quite shocking, and some of his comments, I believed, were racist in nature. He was accusing Muslims of dominating towns with their minarets and their prayers, of breeding faster than it was acceptable to breed. He then described how the populations should be moved around to create some order in the state of Bosnia, as he saw it, and this would involve forcible removal of individuals, regardless of their own wishes, a total interference in their lives by the state, and also included the possibility of the use of the army to enact this process. I was frankly horrified by these thoughts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The book that Mr. Valenta gave to you at that time, was that called "The Partition of Bosnia and the Struggle for Integrity"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During the meeting did Mr. Valenta also show you charts with demographic data that were in his office?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he did. He had a number of charts on the wall, which he displayed as he was going through his briefing on the situation and the solution, as he saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During the discussion, did Mr. Valenta explain to you as well that he had no more friendship, feelings of friendship with the Muslims in the region, that he even felt hatred toward them?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, he did. We talked about his past and his life to date. And it transpired, and I knew this from the cover of his book, apart from anything else, that he had been born in Dolac and had been to school in the local area, alongside both Muslims, Croats and some Serbs. He had then gone off to university and come back and been a teacher. And I think the fact that he had returned to teach young people and held these very strong racist views, I found, to be honest, unacceptable; that somebody with such a good education, a university education, could propose a solution to the problems in his country which involved forcible movement of populations based on their ethnic origin. He further went on, when I questioned him, and I said, "Well, how do you feel about Muslims now?" And he said, "I hate them." Those were his exact words.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did he also tell you that it was out of the question for him to continue living with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he did. He found them intolerable to live with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During the discussion, or after the discussion with Mr. Valenta, did you make a connection between the theories and doctrine that he was expressing with the events taking place in the area around Vitez in April?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did. It wasn't difficult when one looked at the situation in this pocket, in this HVO pocket in the centre of Bosnia, that Valenta had produced, if you like, the doctrine for what was going to happen. Then the policy from that doctrine had been distilled, I believe, by Dario Kordic, who was responsible for the internal affairs. And that policy was then put into effect by the HVO. So you had a doctrine, a plan, and an instrument to carry out exactly what Valenta had proposed, and I was well aware that Valenta was a serious and senior official of the HDZ party. And here was this party proposing to put in effect and had put into effect this policy. And I believed that Ahmici represented a first step along that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: A few days after the meeting with Valenta, that is, the 19th of May, 1993, did you have the opportunity to go to a country house outside of Busovaca where Dario Kordic lived? What was the name that was given or that you gave to that residence at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: At the time we gave the name of the Eagle's Nest to that residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you tell us why that name was given to that location?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: There were a number of factors that led to that name being given, and it was I that gave it that name. It was the first time I had been there. It was set as a hunting lodge in beautiful countryside, and it was a place where political people clearly met. And I made a parallel with events in the past, and therefore it then became known as the Eagle's Nest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The events in the past that you are talking about are Berchtesgaden? Did you think about Berchtesgaden?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That is correct. I saw there was a similar parallel to those two situations, of Berchtesgaden and what became known as the Eagle's Nest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During that meeting on the 19th of May, were Mr. Blaskic and Mr. Valenta both present?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: They were indeed, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you remember some of the subjects that were discussed during those meetings, what was the very specific purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: The purpose of the meeting was to get to know -- or for me to be invited, and I think for people to meet me in the area. I believe the main purpose of that meeting was as a political meeting for the HDZ, because, as far as I could see, most of the senior people were assembled at that meeting. But at the same time, it was also a social meeting where they had obviously gathered for lunch, to which I, and I believe the Dutch battalion commander at the time, Colonel Schipper, had been invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During that meeting did you happen to talk about a safe zone that you were requiring to be around your camp, so as to avoid -- that you would not come under the fire of snipers?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I was -- did not raise many subjects for discussion, since it was clearly a social invitation for lunch, but what I did raise was the problem of both BiH and HVO soldiers firing into the United Nations camp that my troops occupied. And it was my understanding it was an agreement, which had been made with both of these parties in the conflict, that they would observe a 500-metre exclusion zone around my camp, where there would be no military activity and certainly no firing into the camp. The reason I had specifically raised this point, as we had been having HVO sniper fire from the HVO lines to the south of our camp directly into and across our camp, and this was clearly dangerous for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: General Duncan, do you remember any other subjects that may have been discussed during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Not specifically, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Ten days later, that is, the 29th of May, 1993, you and some of your men transported in your vehicles the unit commanders to Kiseljak for a meeting which was being held at the United Nations headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: General Petkovic was also there at that meeting. Could you tell us in a few words what happened during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. I was requested by the United Nations to ferry under armour, for their safety, senior officers from the HVO to a meeting in the United Nations headquarters in Kiseljak. The plan was so that the United Nations could speak to the HVO about events. In the event, what actually happened was that the meeting with the HVO and United Nations lasted some 20 minutes. After that, the HVO officers drove off in their cars and I believe went for a meeting themselves. They returned some three hours later to the U.N. headquarters and I ferried them back to where they had come from, from the Busovaca and Vitez pockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: After that meeting of the HVO unit commanders in Kiseljak, or the Kiseljak region, did you see any developments in the relationship between the HVO and the Serbian forces in the region?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: We began to notice, after that meeting, that there was very little military activity on the front lines between Serb and Croat. And indeed, in the Kiseljak area we became aware that considerable black market activity was taking place across front lines, cigarettes in particular, and also fuel was coming in. In addition to that, as events went across, we noticed that where the HVO had suffered some defeats at the hand of the BiH Army, civilians and, I believe, some soldiers, had actually moved across those front lines with the Serbs and later reappeared, as it were, having moved around. This took place both in the Travnik area, after the expulsion of HVO from Travnik, and the Croats from Travnik, and also in the Vares area later on in the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly by taking it that the borders between the HVO and the Serb forces became more permeable at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Sir, that would be exactly correct. That would be a very succinct way of summing up that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You just told us that you were responsible for transporting some of the unit commanders to Kiseljak, that is, military authorities. Did it sometimes happen as part of your responsibilities you would transport civilian or political authorities, and specifically Dario Kordic and other representatives of the HDZ political party?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: This I in general refused to do, and indeed on a number of occasions Valenta had asked me specifically to move him round, and I refused so to do. There was one occasion later on in the Vance-Owen planning where I was asked to move a number of civilians out of the area to a major meeting that I believe was taking place in the Mostar area. In general, these directives came down from my headquarters of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I would like to show you a document, one dated 24 August 1993, which is reference Z1179. . 1179. Would you look at the page, which, at the bottom, says 5-6, the paragraph that says "Orbats/Personalities." Could you make a comment to us about the request that your regiment received at that time and tell us what is the list that we see in this document.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. This request was to transport, as it says on the bottom of page 5-6, the full Croat political hierarchy in Central Bosnia, and there follows on page 6-6 a complete, as we believe it, or nearly complete, list of the major political figures that existed in Central Bosnia at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: According to the list that was given to you at the time by Mate Boban, or people acting in his name, Dario Kordic appears as the first person on the list in that hierarchy of political authorities in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, he does. He's very much the first on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, that's all right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: We have already mentioned the incidents of the 10th and 11th of June, 1993, these incidents relating to the Convoy of Joy or the Convoy of Mercy, since both of the expressions were used interchangeably for that convoy. You yourself were involved, were the direct witness of the fact that we're going to speak about. The convoy was authorised, that is, its movement was authorised, by an agreement between the Croatian authorities and the Bosnian authorities so that the convoy could reach Tuzla. You were able to see yourself documents that indicated that that agreement had been reached; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. I was shown the documents by Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would appreciate it if the Prosecution would not lead on this particular subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You learned about these documents. Could you tell us how you learned it or where the documents came from, who issued them?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I was concerned about the safety of a convoy, which I knew was coming from the south, consisting of a number of Muslim-driven vehicles which contained supplies and equipment for the Muslims in Tuzla. The convoy was about 300 vehicles, that was the proposed strength, and it contained, I believe, a complete mix of medicines, food, clothing, and aid, in general, for Muslims in the north. We learned about the arrival of this convoy from United Nations sources, and I immediately, having learnt about this, went to see Tihomir Blaskic in his headquarters to confirm that he had received instructions to the effect that the convoy was to get through, and I did that because the United Nations command had told me there was a formal agreement. Commander Blaskic then told me about this formal agreement and showed me the pieces of paper, and I sought his assurances that the convoy would not be harmed and that he would facilitate its passage. This, he stated, he would do to the best of his ability, but he did comment that there were a lot of people in the Vitez pocket, some 30.000 additional displaced people, and that it would be difficult to control them. I said, "As a military commander, it is your responsibility, along with the civilian government, to make sure that the people are controlled. You have that responsibility," which he accepted but reluctantly. That is the background to the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly under what circumstances that convoy was stopped in the Novi Travnik region and then in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: The convoy arrived at the southern edge of the interface between Muslim and Croat forces, which was Gornji Vakuf, and it proceeded up through the Muslim area below Novi Travnik. It then came to an area known, I believe, as Radovica [sic], I think it's called -- I would have to check on that -- it is an area just down below Novi Travnik, where the road from the south at Gornji Vakuf comes out into a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. The name that you're mentioning, might it be Rankovici?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, Rankovici. Thank you. I'm sorry. Yes, it's Rankovici. It was there that the road was blocked and the convoy was forced to halt; it was there that Muslim drivers were extracted from their vehicles and shot, we believe a total of eight. My soldiers were unable to take action at that stage because they were blocked from both seeing this happening directly, although we heard the shots and found the bodies later on, and it was there that that convoy was then looted by soldiers and civilians. I myself was blocked by a crowd of women and children who had moved across the road further to the north of that, as it was my intention to go down and see what was going on and try and resolve the situation. Whilst I was stuck at that roadblock of women and children, trying to get down south, vehicles containing Petkovic, the commander, came down, who spoke to the crowd. I asked for Petkovic for his assistance to get me down south, and he laughed and drove through, leaving me still there. A little later on, two cars of HVO police also came down the road from the north. They stopped again by me at this block of women and children, talked briefly to the women and children. I then asked them to assist me in getting down to the south. They were extremely abusive and they then drove through as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: General, you've just spoken about the HVO police. Is this the civilian or military police?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: This is the military police, and I have seen a video taken by a newsreel team which shows the HVO insignia, belts, batons, and white pistol holders, which indicates the HVO police involved in that activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Excuse me. I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: The convoy then was obviously stuck, and we were negotiating to get it through. Eventually, it was released from that area and then came up into the area of Vitez, where it was blocked again at the junction at the east end of town, on the Vitez bypass where one can turn south or carry on along the road that eventually leads down the Lasva Valley. You will appreciate that a convoy of 300 vehicles is quite a long convoy, and having discovered it had been blocked, I went out with the ECMM ambassador and with Tihomir Blaskic to try and unblock the convoy. It was blocked by local HVO soldiers and women and children. I got to the front of that convoy in my vehicles and demanded that we come through, and I was told that the soldiers and the women and children would not move, except on the express orders of Dario Kordic; I confirmed that a number of times. They were absolutely clear. They were shouting the name "Kordic, Kordic, Kordic," and that was it. They would not in any way speak to Blaskic. Indeed, when I mentioned Blaskic's name, I remember one of them spitting on the ground. We moved off backwards, away from the convoy, back to the ECMM hut, to try and resolve the problem, at which stage I discovered that elements of the convoy had been split off and were being moved by Croats, civilian and military, off the road into the town of Vitez, into the quarry, which is at the beginning of Vitez. Indeed, the whole convoy was being broken up and dispersed round the town and looted by the locals, both civilians and military. I should add that in the course of the movement of the convoy through the Vitez area, two HVO soldiers fired at the convoy, thereby endangering the lives of the drivers, and in order to further protect those lives, my soldiers, in a Warrior, fired their machine gun, which killed those two soldiers. We were now in a stalemate situation where there was no convoy left to look after. I informed and had kept informed the United Nations at all times. The United Nations Chief of Staff, Brigadier Hayes, came down to join me, and the next morning we began work again to undo this problem. I think we then met again at the wood factory, and also in Hotel Vitez, at which time it became apparent that this situation could go on no longer, and I made that point both to Tihomir Blaskic and Dario Kordic. It was Dario Kordic who then said he would sort out the situation, and within an hour, those vehicles had all been released and put back on the road and assembled again; the convoy was then able to move off. I was quite surprised at the speed at which it happened and also quite surprised at the way it was quite clear that it was Dario Kordic who was, as it were, calling the shots for this event and that General Blaskic or Colonel Blaskic was taking the back seat. The convoy eventually moved off, having lost a significant part of its equipment, and people had been killed, and that then closed, if you like, this incident, with the convoy moving out of my area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning of your testimony, General, when you spoke about that event, you spoke about eight people whom you didn't see, but you heard the shots, and eight people were allegedly killed at the beginning of that roadblock. Later on, did you have any information about the execution of those eight individuals?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: We understood, sir, that they had been killed by the HVO or civilians in that area. There were both HVO police in that area and HVO soldiers. It's my understanding that they were killed by weapons held by those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you don't know why those eight people were executed.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I can only assume, sir, that they refused or were very reluctant to give up the contents of their load to anyone else. Having been blocked and then clearly assaulted, pulled out of the cabs, they may well have resisted and that resulted in their being shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
