utterances.text: General Duncan, other drivers, or rather several of the other drivers, those who were not killed, they were also subjected to very grave violence, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: They were, yes. A number of them were beaten up and they sheltered by their vehicles overnight, and we did as best as we could to provide sentries to stop further harassment. Regrettably, another two or three drivers, I believe, were killed up in the area of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You spoke about the quarry, the quarry which is near Vitez. Is it the Mosunj quarry that you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's a very large quarry. It's a very obvious feature on the map. That quarry was where a number of the vehicles which had been looted or were being looted were taken by local police military and civilians, and that's where they were left. And it was there that I went to examine the situation. In fact, there are HVO forces stationed in that quarry. It is in the area where there were a number of, or one or two, large howitzers which fired from the relative safety of the quarry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And that quarry is therefore in the area of responsibility of Mario Cerkez, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It is his area of responsibility as the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And the two HVO soldiers who were killed by your men, why were they killed?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: They were killed because they were firing on the convoy with their rifles, and having fired warning shots, they refused to stop firing and carried on firing. And under my mandate and the rules of engagement, it was clear to us that the only way we could stop them was that they would be shot, or certainly shot at. And unfortunately, both were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And it all happened in the Vitez area, did it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: In the Vitez area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And after your meeting, you talked with the ECMM ambassadors and with Dario Kordic and Colonel Blaskic. What was the interpretation you gave to those events?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Looking at the events as a whole of that two-day period, I concluded that there had been a plan made, despite the orders from, I assume, Mate Boban, to let the convoy through, that a certain slice could be taken off this convoy for the inhabitants of the Vitez pocket to have. And so a certain amount of looting was to be tolerated. I suspect that this explained the reason for the HVO Commander Pektovic to be in the area that day and the day before. I assumed he was consulting with the HVO in that area. I also suspect that perhaps events got out of hand and people took more than, perhaps, had been bargained for. And the plan, as it were, which I believe -- and it is my opinion -- it was a plan to cut out these things. The plan went slightly wrong and more was taken and people were killed when perhaps they shouldn't have been killed. And then finally, when we realised and when the HVO realised things had gone too far, Dario Kordic was very quick to say, "That's it." They had taken their slice and then they would let the convoy through. It was my opinion the whole thing was very neatly and carefully orchestrated. To achieve the results they did in the way they blocked the road at critical places, to cut out those vehicles neatly and accurately in small packets, would have taken a deal of planning. It was a very precise, clever, fast and slick operation, which required a very clear set of orders and a very clear command chain to make sure it went well. And as far as I could see for the Croats in that pocket, that plan did go well. They succeeded in getting what they wanted. It would, of course, have enhanced the reputation of the local commanders in that area with their population, in that they had given them the food and supplies they believed they needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And you exclude the possibility that it was organised by civilians who were furious, they wouldn't let the convoy just get away?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's an excellent excuse, but, as I said, I have seldom seen such a well-orchestrated plan; where we were cut off, there were clear routes to take vehicles away, people could be moved on and off roads, and, as I say, at the end, when Kordic issued the orders to unblock, things were unblocked very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During your meeting with Kordic on the 11th of June, did he say that he would conduct an investigation of the murders of the drivers who had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is in dispute, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Lopez-Terres, don't lead on this particular matter. Brigadier, would you tell us what, if anything, Dario Kordic may have said about an investigation or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Because people had been shot, it is a requirement from my side to produce an investigation as to those details of why they were shot. And this affected all shootings that my soldiers were involved in. And I also asked that the HVO in a similar fashion would produce a report as to why people had been murdered, because, clearly, people had been murdered, and I wished to establish exactly why and how. To my knowledge, this report was never produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And who did you ask to produce the report?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I asked the report to be produced by Dario Kordic. I would accept that it is not necessarily his responsibility to produce that report, but I would expect the HVO command, as it were, to have produced a report to me. They had in the past proven they could produce reports remarkably quickly. We had an event where a rocket launcher was fired into my camp. Within two days, the HVO soldier who had done this was found. He was put on trial. He was found guilty, sentenced, and locked up in Busovaca prison. So I knew they were capable of producing investigations and reports when they felt like it. And I suspect in this instance they didn't feel like it. You could ask that perhaps I should have reminded the HVO government about this, but, to be honest, with the span of command that I had, this became just another problem which clearly wasn't going to have a resolution, and I had to move onto other concerns and business.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: General Duncan, before we round off the testimony regarding the Convoy of Joy, I should like to show you three documents. One is Z1,044. That is 1044. The second is a report which has already been produced. The second one is 1049,1. The third is Z1,091. These are three reports. The first one is of June 11th; the second is the 12th June; and the third of the 21st of June.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm missing the report from the 11th of June. Could I ask for the number again? Thank you. I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could we please have report Z1,044 placed on the ELMO. Will you please quickly read through the report.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I will. I'll read it off the ELMO. It's the military info --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: No. No. No. Just for yourself. Just for yourself. Just read it through. This was the report of your regiment and it recounts the circumstances of the incident. And I believe there is also an annex with the precise chronology of the incident. Could you please have a look at this annex, which is on the last page. Does this tell you what you saw happen and what you were reporting about?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It is a report, obviously, compiled in my headquarters at the same time as I was out dealing with these events. So the accuracy of times is clearly much more accurate than I have been able to describe from my memory. But it does constitute a fairly succinct and full report of the events that took place in those two days, the 10th, 11th of June. The timing, obviously, at the start of each paragraph, the first two figures being the date and then the second four figures the time in a 24-hour clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Eleven means the day?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The second document is dated the 12th of June, paragraph 2. 1049,1. This is passage 2 on the Convoy of Mercy. It again says that the instructions given by Kordic were followed up and obeyed.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And the third report dated the 21st of June, page 6 of the report. There is a passage entitled "Freedom of Movement." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: After the 11th of June, did you once again discuss with General Blaskic -- and to discuss the authority which Dario Kordic evidently had in that area, as evidenced a few days before that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The report of the 21st of June, and this is in relation to a meeting which you had with Colonel Blaskic. And during that meeting, if I understand properly this report, you reminded Blaskic about the incidents of the 11th of June and that it was possible to put an end to it, owing to the intervention of Dario Kordic, who, evidently, could control the movement of the population in the area.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you, usher. We are now passing onto the 19th of June, 1993. That day you organised, General Duncan, a meeting with the authorities of two parties, Colonel Blaskic, Colonel Hadzihasanovic, Colonel Merdan, and the purpose of the meeting was to try to arrive at an agreement on ceasefire and understanding about various issues. And at the time I believe you were the one who drew up a report of that meeting of the 19th of June '93, and which is Z1,078?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I have the document in front of me. It is -- I typed it myself. I typed these documents immediately after meetings of what we called the joint command. And the joint command is really the -- on the last page those individuals who are named as the action addressees. That includes Colonel Blaskic and Colonel Hadzihasanovic, the two senior military commanders in that area on the BiH and Croat sides. The aim of the meeting was very much as in the agenda, those six items there, as these items were disrupting the stability of the area, to say the least. We were moving from a disturbed situation towards open hostility between the BiH and the Bosnian Croat army, the HVO. The important thing about this piece of paper is paragraph 5, where both commanders agreed to those following subparagraphs there, that they would take action and issue orders to make sure they took effect. And you can see from the list there, these are fairly substantial activities I was asking them to do in order to calm down the situation and prevent these events taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: At that time of the meeting there were prisoners too who had been detained equally by the HVO and by the Bosnian army. Could you tell us something as regards the HVO? Where were Muslim prisoners detained?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Muslim prisoners were detained in a number of sites within the HVO area of control. I did not know exactly where these sites were, but the numbers of prisoners were held by the ICRC where they could, and were monitored by the ECMM where they could, and that applies to both HVO and BiH prisoners. Prison exchange was a major feature of this joint command meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Are you aware of Muslim prisoners in the areas of Vitez, Busovaca and Kiseljak at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was. And the numbers were given to me by the BiH and for the HVO prisoners, and for the reverse. As a result of getting those numbers, we decided together, with the commanders present, the ECMM and the ICRC, to get together senior officers from both sides to work out a programme for repatriation of the prisoners from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: At that time too, are you aware of some complaints of the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities regarding the status of prisoners, that is, prisoners made to dig trenches for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: This was a complaint from both the BiH and the HVO, that prisoners on both sides were being made to dig trenches. I did state at the time that just because one side is doing it doesn't give carte blanche to the other side to do it, and I said that it was actually illegal to use prisoners in such a fashion and asked that prisoners should not be doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: After that meeting of the 19th of June, did you also organise other meetings of the same kind with the same participants, or was it because this meeting evidently did not meet with a successful end that you stopped such meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: We continued to organise a series of meetings, but it rapidly became apparent that action was not taking place on either side and, therefore, it was pointless carrying on. To be honest, at that stage, there became a situation of open warfare between the BiH and the HVO in Central Bosnia. So my attempts at mediation had broken down. The inevitable, if you like, had almost been pushed to the right, and open warfare broke out. This represented a period of the maximum activity in that Vitez pocket area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Perhaps just one last item before we conclude for today. We already talked about June 1993, fire was -- rather, a shot was fired at your camp. You complained with Colonel Blaskic about that and Colonel Blaskic assured you very quickly that the person who had fired that shot had been found and detained. Could you briefly recount that incident, please.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Sorry. I could recount it, but I believe I have already recounted it in some detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Sufficiently for our purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a document which bears on this incident. I wanted to show it to the witness. The document is Z1130.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: It is a letter addressed to Colonel Blaskic on the 30th of June, 1993. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have. This was another document that I drafted myself. Thank you for reminding me. Commander Blaskic's response to the incident had been so quick and efficient, I thought it polite, since I demanded the inquest, that I write back and thank him for it, and you can see I have complimented him on the speed and efficiency in which he'd taken that action, offering my thanks for his assistance in unlocking that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: That fire that was opened on your camp came from the area of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, it did. It was initiated by one of the local HVO soldiers, who was subsequently taken off to Busovaca, which is the prison for the local soldiers, and incarcerated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: But you could never ascertain whether that soldier had, indeed, been taken into custody and sentenced. I mean, that was only what Colonel Blaskic told you.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That is entirely correct. I actually thought it somewhat rude to question Commander Blaskic. He'd obviously taken firm action, and as one commander to another, I thanked him, and that was the end of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You believed his word. You never saw a document.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: No, I never saw a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that we could adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn until tomorrow. I said 2.45. It may be more sensible to sit at 3.00 because the previous hearing which I'm involved in will go on until 2.00. So 3.00 tomorrow. We will then sit, provided the interpreters are agreeable, a little more than an hour and a half, sit without a break, I suggest. Brigadier, would you please be back then tomorrow to continue with your evidence. I warn you, as all witnesses are warned, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over; that does include members of the Prosecution. But, as I said earlier, if you need to speak to them about travel arrangements or a day to come back, of course you can do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, thank you very much, and I apologise for not being able to be more flexible in my dates to return. I do apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Brigadier, we're well used to it. Tomorrow at 3.00 please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
